title: Investigative Journalism

jokes.text: Troy describes a video game where you can 'do taxes,' 'don't get audited,' and 'enroll in community college' as the most amazing thing ever
jokes.setup: Troy is hyping up a video game as incredibly cool and immersive
jokes.punchline: The features he lists as amazing are mundane adult obligations — taxes, audits, community college — the exact boring reality the characters live
jokes.explanation: Classic Troy joke — his genuine, childlike enthusiasm for something that is objectively the opposite of cool. The escalating banality of the features (taxes! audits! community college!) is structurally tight and deeply character-integrated. Only Troy would describe enrollment in community college as a game feature without irony. Strong opening note.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Dude, we could be doing quests, unlocking achievements, finding hidden treasure...

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're literally at community college right now.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Vacations are wasted on the young. You guys gotta get out there and see the world at some point or you're gonna miss your entire lives.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is sharing vacation stories; Pierce seems about to dispense wisdom
jokes.punchline: Pierce inverts the famous 'youth is wasted on the young' idiom and delivers it as genuine advice, obliviously
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce — mangling a well-known saying and delivering it with condescending authority. It's competent character comedy but not especially surprising. The inversion works, though it's a relatively well-worn joke type for this character.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I don't know, I blacked out. Do you have pictures?

jokes.text: Pierce reacts to Jeff's guess that he became a grandfather by saying 'No, I became even cooler' — then reveals he got an ironic T-shirt
jokes.setup: Jeff sarcastically guesses Pierce became a grandfather, implying Pierce is old and uncool
jokes.punchline: Pierce doubles down that he became 'even cooler' — the reveal being an ironic T-shirt, which is itself uncool and already dated
jokes.explanation: Solid Pierce characterization — his desperate attempt to be relevant makes the ironic T-shirt reveal a good deflation joke. The setup ('even cooler') elevates the mundane punchline. Mid-tier joke, works because Pierce's obliviousness is consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I became even cooler. I got an ironic t-shirt.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: It says 'World's Best Dad' but I'm not a dad. Get it?

jokes.text: Jeff's cold, declarative introduction: 'Let's get one thing straight. I wish I was still a lawyer, I'm only here because I'm hot for Britta, and I don't want to be anybody's friend.'
jokes.setup: The group is warming up for the new semester; Jeff is about to summarize his personality
jokes.punchline: Jeff delivers a brutally honest, rapid-fire self-assessment with no shame — a perfect capsule of his Season 1 persona delivered as a deadpan monologue
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy and character integration. This three-part confession — law, lust, misanthropy — works as a recap gag for returning viewers and an instant character establishment for new ones. Each clause lands as its own beat. The structure is almost stand-up quality in its precision. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Look, I need to be honest with all of you. Everything I do here, every study group meeting, every adventure we go on... it's all just because I'm trying to get into Britta's pants.

jokes.text: 'Just kidding. Bring it in here, you knuckleheads.' — Jeff immediately undercuts his cold declaration with warmth
jokes.setup: Jeff's ruthless self-summary seemed like a sincere declaration of antisocial intent
jokes.punchline: He immediately invites a group hug, calling them 'knuckleheads' — the reversal reveals his growth while also being funny in its corniness
jokes.explanation: Works as a quick callback deflation of #3. 'Knuckleheads' is an endearingly dorky word choice that underlines Jeff's buried warmth. Dependent on the previous joke for most of its impact, so not fully standalone.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I was just being honest.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: But hey, who wants pizza?

jokes.text: Abed compares Jeff to Hawkeye from M*A*S*H, referencing 'the 11th year of the Korean War'
jokes.setup: Jeff is explaining his new positive attitude about Greendale
jokes.punchline: Abed processes this through a pop culture lens (M*A*S*H), and the specific detail 'the 11th year of the Korean War' is the joke — a reference so arcane and specific it becomes funny on its own
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed joke structure — the pop culture reference isn't random but is thematically apt, and the hyper-specific detail ('11th year') is the comedic topping. It also plants the M*A*S*H thread that pays off beautifully later. Strong character integration for Abed.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The Korean War only lasted 3 years. M.A.S.H. ran for 11 seasons.

jokes.text: Buddy appears mid-group-hug having 'snuck in' — Jeff asks 'Did you just teleport here?'
jokes.setup: The group is having a warm reunion hug; nobody has introduced a new character
jokes.punchline: A stranger is suddenly among them, having infiltrated the hug undetected — the visual of a stranger emerging from a group embrace mid-scene
jokes.explanation: Strong visual gag — the audience can picture the absurdity of Buddy materializing inside a group hug. Jeff's 'Did you just teleport here?' is a good confused reaction line. The physical setup is the main comedy engine.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Buddy? What are you doing here?

jokes.text: Abed is the only one who recognizes Buddy: 'Sits in the corner, next to the dead plant.'
jokes.setup: Nobody recognizes Buddy from Spanish class; he's been invisible to the whole group
jokes.punchline: Abed, as the hyper-observant one, identifies him with eerie precision — but the detail 'next to the dead plant' makes Buddy's social invisibility even sadder and funnier
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words do triple duty: establish Abed's observational superpower, confirm Buddy's sad social status, and add a melancholy comic detail (the dead plant as a companion). Abed could only deliver this. Very tight.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: How did you even get in here?

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: I infiltrated your intimate moment.

jokes.text: Buddy explains he knows them all 'from watching you all last semester grow together' — clearly implying he was a lonely observer/stalker
jokes.setup: Buddy is trying to justify his familiarity with the group
jokes.punchline: His explanation reveals he was watching them grow together from a distance, which is touching but also deeply creepy — the camera likely holds on this
jokes.explanation: Good cringe setup for Buddy's character — the pathos is played for uncomfortable laughs. The implication that he was essentially an invisible watcher is both sad and unsettling, which is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: You guys remember me from Spanish class?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Flash of Buddy's memory/fantasy: Britta getting an F-minus on a test, Annie confessing she cheated, then 'Give me back my bra, Annie' / 'I'm not even wearing a bra'
jokes.setup: Buddy claims to know the group from watching them in class — we flash to his memories
jokes.punchline: His memories are increasingly absurd non-sequiturs: someone cheats, then there's an inexplicable bra dispute — the last line ('I'm not even wearing a bra') is the peak absurdity
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdity of Buddy's memories — from mundane test-taking to the inexplicable bra incident — is nicely structured. 'I'm not even wearing a bra' as the final beat is well-timed deadpan. The whole sequence is funnier on rewatch when you understand Buddy's character.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, Buddy from class. I remember him now.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: There's a dead plant in that corner that makes the whole thing sound extra pathetic.

jokes.text: 'I sleep a lot in class, that one might have been a dream.'
jokes.setup: Buddy has just recounted increasingly bizarre memories of the group
jokes.punchline: He casually acknowledges that the last memory — the bra incident — might not have been real because he sleeps in class; delivered with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy. The line retroactively recontextualizes the previous absurd memory and adds a layer: not only is Buddy a creepy watcher, he may be dreaming about these people. The casual delivery ('that one might have been a dream') is pitch-perfect deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: People don't notice me because of my body type, not my personality.

jokes.text: Buddy spontaneously breaks into a song about wanting to join the group mid-conversation
jokes.setup: Buddy is trying to make a logical argument for joining the study group
jokes.punchline: He interrupts himself with a full musical number — '* I can't count the reasons I should stay *' — the absurdity of bursting into song in a mundane setting
jokes.explanation: Community playing with musical comedy as genre parody. The joke is partly that Buddy uses a musical number as a persuasion tactic mid-sentence. Works best on rewatch when Buddy's whole character arc pays off.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: Yeah, and then Britta got an F on the exam.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Britta cheated?! I can't believe she would cheat!

jokes.text: The Dean lures Jeff with a fake text about 'free Sephora samples' to pitch him the newspaper job
jokes.setup: Jeff receives a mysterious summons to meet someone
jokes.punchline: The Dean used 'free Sephora samples' as bait — implying he correctly judged that this would work on Jeff, which reveals both Jeff's vanity and the Dean's manipulative weirdness
jokes.explanation: Economical character joke that double-dips: it confirms Jeff's vanity (Sephora samples work on him) and the Dean's peculiar fixation on Jeff. 'I have something better than exfoliating soap to rub on you' is a slightly unsettling follow-up that adds to the Dean's creepiness.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: So there was this time Britta lent Annie her bra, right? And Annie's like 'This doesn't fit,' and Britta goes 'Well it fits me fine,' and then Annie says 'Yeah, because you stuffed it with socks!'

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I did not stuff it with socks!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: There were literally five pairs of gym socks in there.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Why are we talking about this?

jokes.text: 'I have something better than exfoliating soap to rub on you. An opportunity.'
jokes.setup: Dean explains the Sephora ruse
jokes.punchline: The phrasing 'rub on you' creates an inadvertently suggestive double entendre; the pause before 'An opportunity' makes it land like a punchline
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean Pelton — the unintentional (or entirely intentional) innuendo is in-character. The beat before 'An opportunity' is structural good timing. The joke works because the Dean's infatuation with Jeff is an established running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: I don't actually remember any of that. I just wanted to impress you guys.

jokes.text: 'This is the first desk I've seen in six months that doesn't have "Zeppelin Rules" carved in it.'
jokes.setup: The Dean shows Jeff the small newspaper office as an incentive to take the editor job
jokes.punchline: Jeff's bar for a 'nice office' is hilariously low — the best he can say is that it lacks Led Zeppelin graffiti, which paints a vivid picture of Greendale's facilities
jokes.explanation: Economical and vivid. The specificity of 'Zeppelin Rules' (not just 'graffiti' — a band whose fans are exactly the type to deface desks) is excellent detail. It characterizes Greendale as a bottom-tier institution while playing Jeff's lowered expectations for laughs. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Buddy, I appreciate your enthusiasm, but I don't think this is going to work out.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: ♪ Why does it have to be this way, why can't we just stay together, why does love always have to... ♪

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Are you... are you singing right now?

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: ♪ Fly away from me! ♪

jokes.text: Jeff as new editor immediately redirects assignments: sends one reporter for pizza, another for a liquor exposé where the goal is 'anything cold and imported'
jokes.setup: Jeff has just been made editor of the school paper and is meeting his eager reporters
jokes.punchline: His 'editorial assignments' are transparently self-serving (food and alcohol for himself) dressed up in journalism language
jokes.explanation: Solid Jeff character moment — his self-interest disguised as mentorship is the core of his Season 1 arc. The joke operates on the audience's expectation that Jeff's 'help' will serve Jeff. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: I'm so excited I could burst! This is the best day ever, and you know what? That rhymes with my name — Buddy, studdy, mud-ee! Get it? I'm just so thrilled to be here, I could buddy-buddy-pal around all day long!

jokes.text: Annie says she's been assigned to edit the crossword 'because I'm a girl' — then immediately adds 'And because I love crosswords'
jokes.setup: Annie complains of being sidelined at the paper for sexist reasons
jokes.punchline: She immediately undermines her own complaint by adding she actually loves crosswords — the self-awareness punctures her indignation
jokes.explanation: Very well structured — the first beat sets up a feminist grievance, the second beat deflates it without dismissing it, which is the comedic sweet spot for Annie's character. The addendum is delivered as an almost involuntary confession. Strong character integration and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I may have exaggerated about those Sephora samples.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: But I'd like to rub some things on Jeff.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Now you love the streets. You're my ace newshound.' — Annie: 'Ace? You can do that?' — Jeff: 'We can do anything we want. It's Greendale.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is playing the hard-boiled editor archetype, assigning Annie to report
jokes.punchline: Annie's disbelief that she can be called 'Ace' is answered with the show's thesis statement — 'It's Greendale' — meaning the low standards of the institution are a loophole for everyone
jokes.explanation: 'It's Greendale' as the ultimate excuse/freedom is a recurring comedic engine for the show and works here as both joke and world-building. Not exceptional on its own but part of a solid scene.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Welcome to the newspaper office, Jeff. State-of-the-art facilities.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Dean, this is a broom closet with a typewriter.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: A very nice broom closet.

jokes.text: Abed continues the M*A*S*H analogy, calling Annie 'Hot Lips Edison' and offering to build Jeff a still for Hawkeye martinis
jokes.setup: Jeff has just played the newsroom scene like a classic Hawkeye moment
jokes.punchline: Abed is fully committed to the M*A*S*H framework, complete with character assignments and prop suggestions — his literal-minded pop culture cosplay is the joke
jokes.explanation: Plants the M*A*S*H thread that pays off beautifully in the episode's climax. Abed's escalating commitment to the framework — now including a still offer — is funny because it's so earnestly specific. Gets a rewatch bonus because the payoff at 17:00 recontextualizes this setup.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Alright everyone, I'm assigning you all to work on an important investigative journalism piece. This is serious work that could expose real wrongdoing.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: The investigation is into which local pizza place gives the biggest slices.

jokes.text: Jeff's response to Abed: 'Of all your pop cultural fixations, this is one I can work with.'
jokes.setup: Abed has just offered an elaborate M*A*S*H framework
jokes.punchline: Jeff's acceptance implies he has been subjected to many, many worse pop culture frameworks from Abed — this one happens to be flattering to Jeff
jokes.explanation: Good economy, a little thin on its own but works in conjunction with the M*A*S*H thread. Jeff's narcissism (he accepts frameworks that cast him as the cool lead) is the subtext.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I need someone to go undercover and investigate illegal underage liquor sales at the local convenience store.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That sounds dangerous. I'll do it.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Actually, I was thinking someone who looks younger. Troy?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm not trying to get arrested.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It's for the greater good. And if it works out, you can keep whatever alcohol you confiscate.

jokes.text: 'Call me Radar?' / 'When you've earned it.'
jokes.setup: Jeff has accepted the M*A*S*H framework; Abed asks for his character assignment
jokes.punchline: Jeff gatekeeps the M*A*S*H nickname as if it's a real honor — 'When you've earned it' played completely straight
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — four words as the punchline. The joke is that Jeff is playing a fictional framework completely straight as if Abed's approval of his M*A*S*H nickname requires genuine merit. The payoff at 18:00 ('Thank you, Radar') is one of the episode's warmest moments, so this gets a rewatch bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: How can you just make stuff up like that?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not making it up. I read it somewhere. Probably.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's not how facts work!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, Annie, Annie. I've been doing this a long time. You develop a sense for what's true. It's called journalistic integrity.

jokes.text: The Dean announces that Señor Chang died over winter break — his moped hit the side of an Arby's
jokes.setup: The Dean is making routine semester announcements
jokes.punchline: He casually announces a teacher's death, specifying the absurd details (moped, Arby's) with zero emotional weight — immediately followed by comfort that 'he did not suffer'
jokes.explanation: Dark humor executed cleanly. 'Moped hit the side of an Arby's' is a perfectly chosen image — undignified, specific, and suburban-tragic. The Dean's equanimity and the class's equanimity are the real joke. Gets a rewatch bonus because Chang obviously doesn't die — this is a pure fake-out.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: This is so sexist! Just because I'm a girl, they assume I love crosswords.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I mean, I do love them, but that's not the point!

jokes.text: 'So sad. / But best semester ever.'
jokes.setup: The class is reacting to the news of Chang's death
jokes.punchline: Brief, sincere-sounding condolence immediately followed by selfish delight — the juxtaposition is the whole joke
jokes.explanation: Five words, two full beats. The transition from 'So sad' to 'But best semester ever' is structurally airtight. Not the most original joke form but executed with maximum economy. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're my ace news hound.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Really? I'm your ace news hound?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's right.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I've never had a cool nickname before!

jokes.text: Chang is alive — enters dramatically, announces 'I am a man who can never die'
jokes.setup: The Dean announced Chang died; the class absorbed the news
jokes.punchline: Chang walks in alive, the death announcement was false, and his entrance monologue ('I am a man who can never die') is characteristically unhinged self-aggrandizement
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed reversal. The death announcement is set up with enough detail (moped, Arby's) to feel like a real plot point, so Chang's entrance is a genuine surprise. 'I am a man who can never die' is perfectly deranged — it's not a denial of the rumor, it's an overblown mythological claim. Chang is introduced at his best.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I have to inform you all that Professor has passed away.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: He was hit by a moped in the Arby's parking lot while trying to retrieve a curly fry that had blown out of his bag.

jokes.text: Chang performs a full rap introducing himself: '* I am Señor Chang / And I'm so ill / This is a warning / I can't be killed *'
jokes.setup: Chang has entered alive after being announced dead; he now needs to establish his new semester persona
jokes.punchline: He delivers a rap — not a parody rap, but a committed, actually-performed rap — as his teacher introduction, escalating the absurdity of his entrance
jokes.explanation: Chang's rap is a great showcase of his character's unhinged self-seriousness. The content ('I can't be killed,' 'in your cabeza') plays on his own mythology. High impact because it's a full comedic performance, not just a line.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Chang is dead. We're free.

jokes.text: Troy, deadpan, after the entire Chang rap: 'Saw that coming.'
jokes.setup: Chang has just performed an elaborate surprise rap entrance
jokes.punchline: Troy's completely flat 'Saw that coming' — which is obviously not true but delivered as though it is — is funnier than any engaged reaction
jokes.explanation: Three words, enormous economy. Troy's particular brand of casual understatement about genuinely surprising things is a great character engine. 'Saw that coming' is funnier because it's so obviously false. Near-perfect economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You fools! Did you really think a mere break could end me? I am immortal! I have walked this earth for centuries, disguised as a security guard at a community college!

jokes.text: 'Saw that coming.' — Deadpan group reaction to Chang's rap
jokes.setup: Chang has just finished an elaborate self-introduction rap
jokes.punchline: Troy's completely flat dismissal — 'Saw that coming' — implies Chang's behavior is so consistent that a rap is not surprising
jokes.explanation: Good punctuation joke. 'Saw that coming' as three words ending a full musical performance is a solid deadpan beat. Troy is well-deployed as a dry reactor.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So we've got the smart one, the hot one, the old one... and Abed, who's just a total weirdo.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Hey!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Sorry, sorry — the weird one. I apologize.

jokes.text: Jeff counts the group: 'three chicks, three dudes, and now two weirdoes' — then apologizes to Abed, 'not all weirdoes are bad'
jokes.setup: The group is debating whether to let Buddy join
jokes.punchline: Jeff's categorization reveals he already mentally classifies Abed as a 'weirdo,' the apology ('not all weirdoes are bad') is a half-measure that makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: Decent character moment — the classification followed by the inadequate hedge ('not all weirdoes are bad') shows Jeff's social honesty and his clueless delivery of backhanded compliments. Good but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You think Buddy could be dangerous? I've thought about this. If Buddy were a serial killer, he'd use a wood chipper. He'd be very specific about it - he'd probably have a whole system. He'd keep detailed notes in a binder, organized by victim profile. The binder would be color-coded.

jokes.text: Abed: 'Buddy might be a puckish agent of change that changes our lives for the better through musical montage. Or he could have a row of jars waiting for our genitals.'
jokes.setup: The group is weighing whether Buddy is benign or a threat
jokes.punchline: Abed presents two mutually exclusive framings — optimistic TV archetype vs. serial killer — with equal calm, the violent escalation landing as pure shock comedy
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is impeccable: two parallel framings, the first optimistic and genre-aware ('puckish agent of change... through musical montage'), the second a sudden, vivid leap into horror ('a row of jars waiting for our genitals'). The specificity of 'jars' (not a vague threat) and the capper 'Yo, I need my genitals' makes it unforgettable. Only Abed can deliver this — he processes the world in genre categories, so the TV-trope framing is natural, and the dark escalation comes from his inability to filter. Highly quotable, became a fan-favorite line.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. So you're just keeping them... in a jar? Like, how often do you check on them? Because if you're not rotating them, they're gonna get all stuck together.

jokes.text: 'Yo, I need my genitals.' — Troy's immediate response to Abed's jar warning
jokes.setup: Abed has just conjured the image of a jar collection for genitals
jokes.punchline: Troy's response is not horror at the concept but a practical, urgent self-interest statement — 'Yo, I need my genitals'
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum comedy. Troy doesn't engage with the absurdist horror — he makes it personal and immediate. The 'Yo' is a perfect register marker (earnest and slightly panicked). Dependent on Abed's setup but executes the callback beautifully. Near-perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I could be a astronaut, but we both know that ship has sailed.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Dealing with problems ain't my job no more. My new job is hanging out, having fun and cracking wise.'
jokes.setup: The group wants Jeff to handle the Buddy situation; Jeff is trying out his new 'relaxed' persona
jokes.punchline: Jeff explicitly names 'cracking wise' as a job title — the meta-awareness of adopting a sitcom sidekick role as a lifestyle choice
jokes.explanation: Good meta joke about Jeff adopting a character archetype as self-improvement. 'Cracking wise' is a funny, slightly dated phrase choice. Sets up his arc for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: A text was sent to all the black students about the concert time change.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: But somehow a random French student named LeBron also got the text.

jokes.text: Shirley's aside — 'Oh, must be nice. Suppose I decide that's my job?' — reaction beat to Jeff's declaration
jokes.setup: Jeff announces his new philosophy of relaxed fun
jokes.punchline: Shirley's dry aside reveals her exhaustion with carrying the group's social weight — the camera presumably holds on her deadpan
jokes.explanation: Functional Shirley beat — she often serves as the voice of exasperated normalcy. Mid-tier but lands.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We should call the number that sent the text.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Why would we do that?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: To find out who sent it.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, no one's dumb enough to answer their own trap call.

jokes.text: Annie discovers the racial profiling text story — the Toni Braxton concert text went exclusively to black students 'and one French kid named Lebron'
jokes.setup: Annie is investigating a story about an anonymous text that helped students at a concert
jokes.punchline: The text went only to black students — an act of racial profiling, however well-intentioned — plus the specific detail 'and one French kid named Lebron' is an absurdist precision that earns a laugh
jokes.explanation: The story itself is a sharp satirical premise (well-meaning profiling), but the comedic gold is 'one French kid named Lebron' — the specificity implies a whole character (a French kid who clearly got grouped in by name association) with zero additional words.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Hello?

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Oh hey Annie! Yeah, I'm just at home... doing normal Dean things. Definitely not in the bushes outside your apartment. Why would you even think that? I'm wearing normal clothes right now, not all black or anything. And this isn't a walkie-talkie, it's a regular phone. A regular phone that I definitely didn't buy at a spy store.

jokes.text: Annie: 'Have you called the number that sent it?' / 'Well, nobody's that stupid, right?' — CUT TO: Dean calling himself back
jokes.setup: Annie is planning a complex investigation into the anonymous text
jokes.punchline: The simplest possible solution (call the number) is dismissed as too obvious — then we immediately cut to proof that it would have worked perfectly, the Dean calling himself back in confusion
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom cut-to structure executed very well. The scene transition IS the joke — 'nobody's that stupid' + immediate evidence that yes, that's exactly how stupid the culprit is. The Dean picking up the phone and stuttering 'Um — Wrong number' is a great visual beat. Strong structural comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Wrong number! Yeah, that's what happened. I dialed wrong. It happens to everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: A very believable mistake. Very natural. Nobody would question that.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: I mean, who hasn't accidentally called someone and then immediately hung up without saying anything? That's totally normal behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Yep. Nailed it. That was my best lie yet.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton answers his own investigative call: 'Hello?' — long pause — 'Um — Wrong number.'
jokes.setup: Annie's investigation has led her to call the number; we cut to the Dean receiving the call
jokes.punchline: The Dean's flustered 'Wrong number' cover — the lamest possible deflection when answering your own phone
jokes.explanation: The 'Wrong number' is funny because it's the worst possible lie when you answer your own phone — there is no wrong number if it's your phone. The beat between 'Hello?' and 'Wrong number' (the visible flop sweat) is where the comedy lives.

jokes.text: Buddy's overly enthusiastic speech thanking the group: 'Thank you guys real much—' then self-correcting 'Real much? Duh.'
jokes.setup: Buddy is trying to deliver a heartfelt speech of gratitude to the study group
jokes.punchline: His nervousness causes him to say 'real much' — a non-phrase — and he calls himself out on it mid-speech
jokes.explanation: Decent cringe beat — Buddy's social anxiety manifesting in a linguistic error. 'Real much? Duh.' is endearing. Mid-tier joke, more character work than pure comedy.

jokes.text: Buddy interrupts Spanish study with a song: '* Annie got an essay portion / Annie gonna move her luscious fanny all day long *'
jokes.setup: The group is trying to study for a Spanish essay
jokes.punchline: Buddy spontaneously sings a song about Annie that sexualizes her — unprompted, escalating, and deeply inappropriate
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe-comedy moment — Buddy's social obliviousness reaches a new level. The song is committed enough to be fully uncomfortable. Sets up the group's response perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: Ay, ay, ay, Annie, you're so fine, so fine, so fine. Ay, ay, ay, Annie, you're on my mind, my mind, my mind. I want to take you to the fiesta, show you my best-a, if you know what I mean, ay, ay, ay!

jokes.text: 'Annie's pretty young, we try not to sexualize her.' — Jeff's flat response to Buddy's Annie song
jokes.setup: Buddy has just sung a song about Annie's body
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response isn't outrage — it's a calm house rule delivered like a style guide note; the deadpan 'we try' implies they've had to establish this policy previously
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest lines in the episode. 'We try not to sexualize her' is funny on three levels: (1) the institutionalized nature of the rule ('we try'), (2) the word 'try' implying it's an ongoing struggle, and (3) Jeff's flat delivery as if this is a normal workplace policy. It's simultaneously an acknowledgment of the show's own tension around Annie and a great character-specific joke. Only Jeff could deliver this as a bored managerial note. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, so that happened. And before you ask, no, we're not going to address it. We're just going to move on like it never happened. Because that's what we do here.

jokes.text: Buddy pitches: 'You guys need a chubby, agile guy. Did anyone see Paul Blart: Mall Cop? I'm like that.'
jokes.setup: Buddy is making his case for why the group needs him
jokes.punchline: His pitch is that he resembles a critically-panned mall cop movie — not aspirationally but matter-of-factly — as a selling point
jokes.explanation: Good self-deprecating character moment — Buddy's reference point for himself is a movie that wasn't a cultural pinnacle. The mispronunciation ('Paul Blart: Marl Car—') followed by his self-correction adds an extra beat. 'I'm fat and I'm physical' as a resume line is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: You know what this group needs? A more sophisticated approach to ironic catchphrase deployment. See, what you're doing is you're using phrases that are inherently contradictory to their surface meaning, but you're not accounting for the meta-textual layer of self-awareness that makes the irony actually function. You need to establish a baseline of sincerity first, then subvert it with calculated insincerity, while simultaneously maintaining just enough earnestness that observers can't tell if you're being genuine or not. That's the sweet spot.

jokes.text: Buddy demonstrates his 'agility' with a high kick — accidentally kicks Jeff in the face
jokes.setup: Buddy is boasting about being 'fat and physical' and able to kick
jokes.punchline: He attempts to prove it with a kick, which immediately injures the group's most valued member — the demonstration backfires spectacularly
jokes.explanation: Classic physical comedy setup — a character boasting about physical skill immediately failing at it. Reasonably well-executed; the injury being a 'nosebleed' rather than something more dramatic keeps it light. The kick will become a running gag.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Just a little nosebleed, I get them when it's dry, or when my face gets kicked.'
jokes.setup: Jeff has just been kicked in the face by Buddy and is bleeding
jokes.punchline: He lists 'when my face gets kicked' as a routine, known trigger for nosebleeds — implying this has happened before — delivered with complete calm
jokes.explanation: The structure here is excellent: 'dry' is a normal nosebleed trigger, so the second cause ('when my face gets kicked') lands as an absurd escalation that Jeff treats as equally mundane. The implication that this is a known recurring condition is very funny. High economy — the whole joke is in the list structure. Excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: I can kick.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: Watch this.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Ow!

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I can't stop thinking about his high kick. His ratio of girth to hip flexibility is mesmerizing.'
jokes.setup: The group is debating Buddy's merits; Pierce is supposed to be analyzing group dynamics
jokes.punchline: Pierce's argument for keeping Buddy is entirely about the physical spectacle of a fat man's flexibility — delivered with pseudo-intellectual phrasing ('ratio of girth to hip flexibility')
jokes.explanation: Pierce's reason for supporting Buddy is hilariously shallow and weirdly specific. The clinical framing ('ratio of girth to hip flexibility') elevates what could be a simple insult into something funnier. Good character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I got a nosebleed from getting kicked in the face.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: It happens.

jokes.text: Pierce pushes for 'Gary' — a friend who 'was raised in Finland, he doesn't get our humor'
jokes.setup: Shirley proposes adding her friend Gary to the group
jokes.punchline: Pierce dismisses Gary because 'he was raised in Finland, he doesn't get our humor' — an absurdly specific cultural excuse that also exposes Pierce's xenophobia and self-aggrandizement
jokes.explanation: Pierce's casually dismissive reason ('he doesn't get our humor') is funny because it assumes the group has a culturally specific comedy sensibility worth protecting, and that Finland specifically would be incompatible. Good Pierce characterization.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: My friend Gary is really nice. You should meet him.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Gary? What kind of name is that? Sounds foreign.

jokes.text: Pierce escalates: 'Gary is off the table. He is a buzzkill. He grew up in a land without sun.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is ranting against Shirley's friend Gary
jokes.punchline: 'A land without sun' as a final condemnation — geographically inaccurate (Finland has sun) but poetically delivered as a devastating character flaw
jokes.explanation: Pierce's escalation from 'doesn't get humor' to 'land without sun' is a good character beat. The phrase 'land without sun' has an almost mythological weight that's funnier than a geographic fact would be.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know what they say - he's got a few screws loose. In my day, we just called it being a Jew.

jokes.text: Secret vote where everyone covers their eyes but speaks their vote out loud — Troy points out 'We'll know each other's voices'
jokes.setup: Jeff proposes a secret vote for Buddy's membership
jokes.punchline: The voting mechanism is hilariously broken — covering eyes doesn't create anonymity when votes are spoken aloud; Troy's calm identification of the logical flaw is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Good logical-absurdism joke. The escalation of a flawed system being implemented without anyone catching the flaw until Troy's simple objection is structurally clean. 'Troy's got a point' as the acknowledgment is a nice beat. The whole exchange characterizes the group's chaotic decision-making.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Buddy's physical comedy is a masterclass in pratfall timing. The way he commits to each stumble—there's a geometric perfection to his falls. He's not trying to be funny; he's achieving comedy through pure kinetic geometry. It's like watching a Buster Keaton algorithm.

jokes.text: Troy: 'We won't know the result. Say your vote out loud. We'll know each other's voices. Troy's got a point.'
jokes.setup: Jeff proposes the nonsensical secret vote system
jokes.punchline: Troy immediately identifies the fatal flaw; Jeff agrees — 'Troy's got a point' — in a rare moment of deference
jokes.explanation: Jeff acknowledging Troy is correct is itself a small joke. The logic is stated clearly and efficiently. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Gary, you're fired.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. He's not a bad guy. He just has a lot of personal problems. His wife left him, he's going through a custody battle, he's got a gambling addiction, and he may have committed a felony.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Shirley, that doesn't help.

jokes.text: Jeff fabricates a news story about a Seattle man killing his driver's ed class with a meat tenderizer to distract the group from the vote
jokes.setup: Jeff needs to derail the vote so he can remove Buddy without a democratic outcome
jokes.punchline: He invents an absurdly specific mass murder story on the fly — 'meat tenderizer,' 'driver's ed class' — the specificity implies he's done this before
jokes.explanation: Jeff's manipulation tactic being a fake sensationalist story is good character work. 'Meat tenderizer' is the right level of specificity — not so implausible it fails, but specific enough to be comedically vivid. 'We have to be careful' as the horrified group response sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Finland is a magical frozen wonderland where the Northern Lights dance across the sky like ethereal spirits, and the people are so pure-hearted that they've never even heard of crime!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: The lakes are so pristine they reflect the very soul of God, and the reindeer roam free in forests of ancient pine, untouched by the cruelty of the modern world!

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: It's a place where sorrow itself is banished, where darkness cannot penetrate the eternal light of human goodness!

jokes.text: Annie confronts Jeff: 'You lied about the guy in Seattle with the meat tenderizer. You put your thumb on the scale. You did it with a smile so you could keep smiling. You're Hawkeye.'
jokes.setup: Jeff has just successfully manipulated the vote through deception
jokes.punchline: Annie's accusation culminates in 'You're Hawkeye' — which is meant as an observation, not an insult, and Jeff's realization that the M*A*S*H framework actually works as a critique
jokes.explanation: Smart comedy-drama hybrid moment. The accusation 'You're Hawkeye' is funny because it recontextualizes the M*A*S*H framework as a critique rather than a compliment — and because Jeff was openly pursuing the Hawkeye persona. Good payoff for the episode's running thread.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, before we vote, I have something important to share. I found this article about Buddy online.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: It says here that he's actually a former convict who ran an illegal pyramid scheme.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, where did you find this?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: The internet. It's definitely real. I definitely didn't make it up in the last five minutes.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton's confession: 'Racial profiling may not be right, but it can be economical.'
jokes.setup: The Dean is confessing to Annie that he sent the racially targeted text
jokes.punchline: His defense isn't denial or apology — it's a cost-benefit argument: profiling is economically defensible when you have limited texts before your rate triples
jokes.explanation: Exceptional line. The Dean's defense of racial profiling on grounds of mobile phone economics is a perfect satirical absurdity — it's both a sharp commentary on how systemic bias can be rationalized by efficiency arguments AND a genuinely funny Dean Pelton moment. The delivery context (his texting rate was about to triple) makes the logic weirdly compelling, which is what makes it dark comedy rather than just offensive. Near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: Annie tells the Dean: 'Tell me, dean, when I refer to you in my article, would you prefer imbecile or incompetent?' Dean: 'I'd prefer incompetent, but what I really want--' Annie: 'It doesn't matter what you want.'
jokes.setup: Annie is in full reporter mode confronting the Dean.
jokes.punchline: The Dean earnestly chooses between the two insults ('I'd prefer incompetent'), treating a loaded rhetorical question as a genuine preference survey — revealing his obliviousness. Annie immediately cuts him off, completing her power move.
jokes.explanation: The Dean earnestly preferring 'incompetent' over 'imbecile' — taking the insult-choice question at face value — is perfect character comedy. It reveals his total lack of awareness that both are terrible. Annie's 'It doesn't matter what you want' is the perfect power pivot, turning her into a parody of a hard-boiled investigative journalist. Both characters are firing on all cylinders here.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're doing the Hawkeye thing again.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What Hawkeye thing?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The thing where you manipulate everyone without them knowing it. It's your signature move. Clint Barton does it all the time in the comics. He's the only Avenger without superpowers, so he has to be smarter and sneakier than everyone else.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm nothing like Hawkeye.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You literally just did it to Buddy.

jokes.text: Dean: 'I'm the least racist person in the world. My best friend when I was 6 years old was a black man.'
jokes.setup: The Dean is continuing to defend himself against Annie's accusation
jokes.punchline: The 'some of my best friends' defense, with the disqualifying detail that the friend was from childhood and is not in his life now — the specific age '6' making it funnier
jokes.explanation: Classic 'some of my best friends' satire, elevated slightly by the specificity ('when I was 6 years old') which makes it even more dated as a defense. The form is well-worn but executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Look, I know profiling is wrong, but do you have any idea how much it costs to text message a minority?

jokes.text: Annie tells Jeff her plan to use the story for journalism scholarships so 'nobody will care about my time in rehab if they think I'm a writer'
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to talk Annie out of running the story
jokes.punchline: Annie casually mentions her rehab past mid-argument as if it's a normal résumé item — the reveal is played deadpan
jokes.explanation: Good character-comedy beat — Annie's backstory (overachiever who had a breakdown and went to rehab) is treated as a breezy aside, which is both funny and characterizing. The logic 'nobody will care about rehab if they think I'm a writer' is beautifully Annie: the solution to one problem is the achievement of another credential.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Dean Pelton, for my article, I need you to choose: are you more of a spineless yes-man, or a craven boot-licker?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Why do I have to choose? Can't I be both?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's... actually perfect for the article.

jokes.text: 'This is Greendale, Jeff, we can do whatever we want.' — Annie echoing Jeff's earlier line back at him
jokes.setup: Jeff used this exact logic earlier to convince Annie to pursue a story
jokes.punchline: Annie weaponizes Jeff's own reasoning against him — the callback is clean and character-appropriate
jokes.explanation: Sharp callback — Annie using Jeff's earlier manipulation against him is a satisfying structural payoff. It also characterizes Annie as sharper than she's given credit for. Clean economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm not racist. I have a very diverse friend group. In fact, when I was a kid, my best friend was Black.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: His name was Reggie. We did everything together. We were inseparable.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Then one day he just... disappeared. Never saw him again.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: So you see? I'm not racist at all.

jokes.text: Buddy has apparently been singing an apology song to the group between scenes — the group missed it and he has to recap it
jokes.setup: Nobody told Buddy he was voted out; he composed and performed an apology song
jokes.punchline: Jeff and presumably others missed the song entirely, forcing Buddy to explain what it was — the fact that he composed a full apology song for a group that wasn't listening is tragicomically absurd
jokes.explanation: Good sustained absurdism — Buddy going to the effort of a full apology song to an absent audience is both funny and sad. The reveal that nobody told him he was out lands as a secondary punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, you need to drop this story. It's not worth it.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Not worth it? Jeff, you're the one who said 'A real journalist follows the truth wherever it leads, even if it destroys everything.' So which is it?

jokes.text: 'My lord, my lady, you missed my apology song.' — Jeff: 'Yeah, I'll-- I'll tell them about it later.'
jokes.setup: Buddy is lamenting that the group missed his elaborate apology
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'I'll tell them about it later' is a completely flat non-commitment that treats the apology song as a minor administrative item
jokes.explanation: Jeff's total dismissal of the elaborate apology song with a vague 'I'll tell them about it later' is good deadpan. The gap between Buddy's investment and Jeff's response is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: I tried joining the study group, they said no. I tried the paintball games, I got eliminated first. I even tried sitting at their table in the cafeteria and they moved.

jokes.text: Jeff's prolonged awkward pause before delivering the bad news to Buddy — 'Buddy, yesterday, the group took a vote... [long pause] ...And you seem to have figured out the rest of it.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is tasked with telling Buddy he was voted out
jokes.punchline: Jeff builds to the news, then trails off and lets Buddy figure it out himself — the pause is the punchline, implying Jeff can't bring himself to say the words
jokes.explanation: Good awkward silence deployed well. Jeff's inability to complete the sentence and outsourcing the conclusion to Buddy is both characteristically Jeff (avoiding direct emotional confrontation) and funny in its cowardice. The extended pause before 'you seem to have figured out the rest of it' is good timing.

dialogue.line: I need more context about the specific punchline text to accurately attribute speakers in this Community scene. The character "Buddy" is not a main character in Community, so either this may be a guest character or there may be a name variation. Could you provide the actual dialogue text from the punchline?

jokes.text: Buddy: 'Was it the high kick? Was it, "You go, girl?"' — cataloguing possible reasons for his rejection
jokes.setup: Buddy is absorbing the news that he was voted out
jokes.punchline: He lists his two most embarrassing moments as the likely culprits — which is accurate — delivered with the saddest possible self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Decent callback moment — Buddy's sad self-inventory is both funny and character-revealing. The irony that the high kick was what KEPT people interested (Pierce loved it) adds a layer.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: These lemon squares represent years of my life, my heart, my soul poured into every bite.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, they're a little dry.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Maybe a little less sugar next time.' — in response to Buddy's lemon squares
jokes.setup: Buddy reveals he made the group lemon squares with free-range eggs as a gesture; clearly worked very hard on them
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response to this heartfelt gesture is a casual note about the recipe — not unkind, but completely tone-deaf to the emotional weight
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff deflection — responding to emotional sincerity with practical critique. 'Maybe a little less sugar next time' is delivered with the perfect register of someone who actually tastes the baking note as useful feedback, not cruelty. Very economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: Buddy: 'Well, I'm not leaving.' — Jeff: 'Oh, come on. Be relaxed, like me. Leave.' — Buddy: 'You're not relaxed. You're an uptight puppet master. And these are your little puppets.'
jokes.setup: Jeff tries to use his 'new Jeff' relaxed persona to defuse the situation
jokes.punchline: Buddy immediately sees through it — 'you're an uptight puppet master' — which is accurate and Jeff knows it
jokes.explanation: Buddy puncturing Jeff's facade is thematically important and mildly funny. 'Uptight puppet master' is a decent insult. The scene does important character work but the comedy is secondary to the plot here.

jokes.text: Buddy: 'Make me, Hitler.' — to Jeff's reasonable request for him to leave
jokes.setup: Jeff calmly asks Buddy to leave; Buddy refuses
jokes.punchline: 'Make me, Hitler' — an escalation from reasonable plea to Nazi comparison in one sentence, the absurdity of the insult disproportionate to the offense
jokes.explanation: Three words, enormous comedic swing. 'Make me, Hitler' as a response to being politely asked to leave is a perfect escalation joke — the disproportionality of the Hitler invocation for a low-stakes social situation is the whole joke. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: You're like Hitler.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, first of all, that's not a fair comparison. Second of all, what do you want?

jokes.text: Jeff's response to Buddy refusing to leave: 'since Buddy's not leaving, he'll just be the person who we wish wasn't here while we study'
jokes.setup: Buddy has refused all requests to leave; Jeff is out of options
jokes.punchline: Jeff reframes the situation with bureaucratic resignation — Buddy has a new official status: 'person we wish wasn't here'
jokes.explanation: Jeff's ability to reframe defeat as a policy position is a great character moment. The bureaucratic precision of 'the person who we wish wasn't here' as a formal designation is very funny. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: No, no, no, NO! This is not happening! I can't— I can't find the book! The book doesn't exist!

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: ¡Ay, Dios mío! ¡No puedo! ¡No puedo!

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: *collapses on floor, flailing* This is my life now! My life is OVER!

jokes.text: Extended scene: Buddy stubbornly studies alongside the group despite being asked to leave — the group eventually physically leaves the library table, and Buddy screams 'No! I want to study with you guys! No!'
jokes.setup: The group has tried everything to get Buddy to leave; they resort to leaving themselves
jokes.punchline: Buddy's escalating emotional breakdown — screaming at the departing group, culminating in 'I hate you! I hate your study group! I hate it! You suck!' — is played as pure cringe spectacle in a public library
jokes.explanation: Good escalation sequence — the full cringe arc of Buddy going from plaintive to unhinged is funny in context. The specificity of 'I hate your study group' as a curse is funny. The whole sequence benefits from Jack Black's (Buddy's actor) commitment.

dialogue.speaker: Security Guard
dialogue.line: Sir, you need to leave the study room.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: No! No, I can't leave! These are my friends!

dialogue.speaker: Security Guard
dialogue.line: I'm going to have to remove you.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait—

jokes.text: Jeff's aside after removing Buddy: 'And you are not running that story.' / 'Why not?' / 'Because I said so.'
jokes.setup: Jeff has just heroically dragged a screaming man from the library
jokes.punchline: He immediately pivots to silencing Annie's journalism as if the two moments are equivalent exercises of authority
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Jeff's power move immediately following physical exertion is funny in its combination of exhausted authority. 'Because I said so' as editorial policy is appropriately self-satirizing.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Leadership isn't about being the best archer or having the coolest outfit. It's about making decisions that affect people's lives, and being willing to live with the consequences of those decisions. Hawkeye doesn't have that burden because he's not real.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Exactly the way I would've done it.' — reaction to Jeff's Buddy removal
jokes.setup: Jeff asks if anyone has a problem with his handling of the Buddy situation
jokes.punchline: Pierce endorses the removal with false expertise, as if his opinion adds validation — the joke is that Pierce's endorsement is the least meaningful possible
jokes.explanation: Functional Pierce beat but one of the weaker jokes in the episode. The joke is too thin — it's just Pierce being self-important with no real twist.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You're special to me, Jeff.

jokes.text: 'Who are you kidding, Abed? I just dragged a screaming, crying man out of a library with his pants down.'
jokes.setup: Abed has apparently called Jeff 'Hawkeye'; Jeff is in self-reflective mode after the Buddy incident
jokes.punchline: Jeff's self-assessment via the most specific detail: 'with his pants down' — a detail not established in the transcript, implying Buddy's breakdown was even worse than depicted
jokes.explanation: The 'with his pants down' detail is a great retroactive reveal — it implies the library scene was even more chaotic than shown, which is funnier than what we witnessed. Jeff's matter-of-fact delivery of this fact as self-deprecating evidence is good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You called me Radar. That's a reference to M*A*S*H. Radar O'Reilly was the company clerk who could predict things before they happened. I've been waiting for you to call me that since the pilot episode. I've mentally prepared a response. I was going to be cool about it, but I'm too excited. I can feel my pupils dilating. Is this what happiness feels like? I think I might cry. Not sad tears, but the kind of tears that come from the intersection of validation and pop culture recognition. I've watched M*A*S*H forty-seven times. Forty-seven. And now you've acknowledged that I'm like Radar. This is the best day of my life since the day you said 'Cool. Cool cool cool.'

jokes.text: Abed delivers the M*A*S*H lecture: Hawkeye 'had blood sprayed on his face and barked orders when the choppers came in. If he didn't, people died. He was a leader, Jeff. That's your job.'
jokes.setup: Jeff claims he doesn't know M*A*S*H; the whole Hawkeye analogy seemed like flattery
jokes.punchline: Abed's correction reveals that the analogy was always a critique, not a compliment — Hawkeye's 'fun' was bought with actual responsibility, and Jeff has been enjoying the martinis without the leadership
jokes.explanation: This is the structural payoff of the entire episode's comedic framework. The M*A*S*H thread has been running since minute 1 as seemingly just Abed's quirky pop culture fixation — here it resolves as the thesis statement of the episode's character arc. The comedy comes from the inversion: what seemed like flattery ('you're Hawkeye!') was always a warning. 'If he didn't, people died' lands as both funny (blood sprayed on face is vivid) and genuinely earned dramatic comedy. Only Abed could deliver this — it requires his pop culture literalism to function. High earned_vs_cheap because it's been built all episode.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Why do we call you Radar?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Because I have an uncanny ability to sense things before they happen.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's actually pretty cool.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, there's a downside. Every time I sense something bad is about to happen, I get an inappropriate physical reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What kind of reaction?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I get an erection.

jokes.text: Annie tells Jeff: 'I never want to be the reason you're mad, because you're Jeff Winger. So thanks for getting mad.'
jokes.setup: Jeff apologized for yelling at Annie about the story
jokes.punchline: Annie subverts the apology by thanking him — the logic being that Jeff Winger losing his temper means he genuinely cares, which is worth more than his normal smooth detachment
jokes.explanation: More comedy-drama hybrid. The joke is in the inversion — being thanked for getting mad. Annie's read of Jeff's character is shrewd and characterizing. Gets rewatch bonus for the Jeff/Annie relationship dynamic it establishes.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: What we need is a good old-fashioned drive-by. Nothing says 'back off' like a drive-by.

jokes.text: 'Thank you, Radar.' / 'Ooh. You made me so happy I just peed a little.'
jokes.setup: Jeff finally confers the M*A*S*H nickname on Abed, earning it through genuine growth
jokes.punchline: Abed's reaction — 'You made me so happy I just peed a little' — is a perfect tonal collision: a sincere, earned moment of Jeff growth deflated by Abed's clinical overshare
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. The callback to 'When you've earned it' at minute 5 is finally paid off here — the whole M*A*S*H thread has been building to Jeff actually earning it, and the moment is simultaneously heartfelt and immediately deflated. Abed's 'I just peed a little' is both totally in character (he processes joy physically and reports it without filter) and the perfect tonal reset. The structure — emotional peak + involuntary bodily function admission — is a textbook Community beat: warmth undercut by clinical absurdism. Near-perfect execution.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Wait, why wasn't I picked?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, Shirley, you're a wonderful woman, but let's be honest—you'd probably try to bake the heist.

jokes.text: Jeff's emergency plan: 'Annie, you flash your breasts as a decoy for the bum-rush.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is strategizing how to handle Buddy's return as a 'crazy stalker'
jokes.punchline: His tactical plan involves Annie using her body as a decoy — inappropriate and immediately criticized
jokes.explanation: The joke is Jeff's casual inappropriate appropriation of Annie's body for tactical use — it's character-consistent but the concept (breasts as decoy) is a bit broad. Gets partially redeemed by the immediate Pierce followup.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Buddy! We've been looking everywhere for you!

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: Yeah, well I found something better.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Better than what? Us?

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: Better than Greendale. Better than all of you.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Dude, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: I found a real community. One that doesn't fall apart every other week.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Britta, don't be upset. I didn't pick you as a decoy because your breasts are so old.'
jokes.setup: Jeff assigned Annie, not Britta, as the decoy — Pierce attempts to explain why Britta wasn't chosen
jokes.punchline: Pierce tries to spare Britta's feelings by explaining she was excluded because of age-related breast concerns — which is both more insulting and more ridiculous than saying nothing
jokes.explanation: Pierce's attempt at consolation making things dramatically worse is a good structure. 'Your breasts are so old' as an explanation for exclusion from an absurd tactical plan is exactly Pierce's brand of unfiltered offensiveness-masked-as-gallantry. Character integration is high.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, so he chose them over us. That's fine. That was actually part of my plan.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I wanted him to think he had a choice.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I didn't pick you as a decoy because your breasts are so old.' — to Britta
jokes.setup: Britta objects to Pierce not selecting her for the breast-decoy plan
jokes.punchline: Pierce's explanation — that Britta's breasts are 'too old' — is both a Pierce-level insult and a logical extension of his terrible worldview; the fact that Britta was apparently upset at being excluded from this role adds absurdity
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce — the insult is specific and delivered with earnest concern ('I didn't pick you because...' as if doing her a favor). The secondary joke that Britta was apparently annoyed at not being selected for the breast-decoy role reverses expectations. Good character integration.

jokes.text: 'Why is he even here? Hello. I invited him.' — the reveal that Jeff himself invited Buddy back
jokes.setup: Buddy has reappeared after being expelled; the group is confused and annoyed
jokes.punchline: Jeff — who expelled him — is the one who invited him back, the reversal of his entire stance played as a simple, almost embarrassed admission
jokes.explanation: Good reversal — the character who made the most noise about Buddy leaving being the one to bring him back is structurally satisfying. The delivery ('Hello. I invited him.') is a good beat — Jeff owning the reversal with mild embarrassment.

jokes.text: Jeff's speech: 'Buddy's crime is thinking we're cool. But I get it. If I were him, and I missed out on you guys, I'd be sitting in that classroom, watching, wondering. So how can I exclude someone from something that I'm so lucky to have.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is explaining why he invited Buddy back after expelling him
jokes.punchline: The speech is sincere and moving — but the joke is that Jeff is making an earnest 'it's not cool to exclude people' speech while two seconds earlier he was plotting a 'bum-rush' using Annie's breasts as a decoy
jokes.explanation: More comedy-drama — Jeff's earnest speech is the character payoff but it's also funny because of the rapid tonal reversal from tactical violence to emotional generosity. The gap between who Jeff is trying to be and who he actually is collapses in a good way here.

jokes.text: Buddy is accepted into the group — then immediately reveals the group was his 'safety,' implying he had better options all along
jokes.setup: The whole episode has been about Buddy desperately wanting to join this group
jokes.punchline: The moment he's accepted, he reveals the group was only his 'safety' — he had a better group all along — the entire episode's premise is punctured retroactively
jokes.explanation: One of the best structural jokes in the episode. The entire A-plot of the episode — Buddy desperately wanting to join, Jeff's internal debate, the vote, the tearful expulsion, the reconciliation — is revealed as moot because Buddy had a better group waiting. The deflation of the whole premise in one word ('safety') is excellent structure. Only works because the show has earned the deflation. The rewatch value is enormous because the whole Buddy arc reads differently knowing this endpoint.

jokes.text: Jeff's talking head/aside: 'And that, ladies and gentlemen, is why I voted to keep him.' — delivered directly after Buddy reveals the group was his safety
jokes.setup: Buddy has just revealed the group was his safety school, undermining the emotional resolution
jokes.punchline: Jeff breaks the fourth wall with a satisfied 'that's why I did it' — implying he voted for Buddy not out of generosity but because he knew Buddy wouldn't stay
jokes.explanation: Perfect. Jeff's aside reveals that his apparent character growth (inviting Buddy back) was actually strategic — he voted for Buddy because he anticipated Buddy would leave anyway. It's the ultimate Jeff Winger move: doing the right thing for the wrong reason, or in this case doing the apparently right thing BECAUSE he knew it would resolve itself. Excellent character integration — this is the most Jeff Winger thing possible.

jokes.text: Pierce immediately says 'It would have been nice to have another person in the group. I'll call Gary.' — the moment Buddy leaves
jokes.setup: Buddy has left for his cooler group; the study group is processing
jokes.punchline: Pierce pivots immediately to his Gary agenda — the entire Buddy debate is now moot and he uses the opening to push his original proposal
jokes.explanation: Good callback — Pierce's opportunism is characteristically immediate. 'I'll call Gary' as his first thought after the Buddy situation resolves nicely closes the Gary subplot loop.

jokes.text: Pierce and Gary present themselves to the group as a 'twosome' — the Dean notes 'I don't see that as a selling point'
jokes.setup: Pierce has brought Gary to pitch to the group; they present as a package deal
jokes.punchline: The Dean observes that two boring people presented as a bundle is a negative pitch
jokes.explanation: Decent joke but thin — it's mostly setup for the Gary subplot resolution. The Dean's dry observation is functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Pierce shows Gary's application 'tape' — the group passes on Gary; 'I don't pop on video.' / 'Let me do the song in person.'
jokes.setup: Gary is auditioning for the study group via video tape
jokes.punchline: Gary has a prepared song for his application but 'doesn't pop on video' — the absurdity of a full study group audition process with video submissions and song performances
jokes.explanation: Good meta-joke about how absurd the whole Buddy A-plot was — the group now has a formal audition process with video submissions. 'I don't pop on video' is a great character detail for Gary (clearly not photogenic but somehow believes an in-person song would change things).

jokes.text: Pierce to the departing group: 'You traitors! I am appalled at your lack of loyalty. Yeah, you better run.'
jokes.setup: The group has voted to pass on Gary; Pierce is furious
jokes.punchline: Pierce's outrage escalates to 'Yeah, you better run' — a threat that makes no sense in this context, delivered with total conviction
jokes.explanation: Classic Pierce escalation — his injury turns to absurd tough-guy posturing. 'Yeah, you better run' as a threat when people are just leaving normally is funny in its incongruity.

jokes.text: Gary's rap pitch: '* Getting rid of Britta / Getting rid of the B / She's a GDB / She's a no-good B *'
jokes.setup: Gary is performing his song to try to get into the group despite being passed on
jokes.punchline: His pitch strategy is a rap attacking one of the group's existing members — the worst possible membership pitch — delivered while the group is walking away
jokes.explanation: Excellent episode-closing joke. The whole arc of 'boring Gary from Finland' has been built up as a foil for Buddy's charisma — but Gary's big song reveals he's not boring, he's just strategically terrible. Rapping to attack a current member as his application pitch is so wrong it's perfect. The 'GDB' (the show's first venture into this running gag concept) is a good detail. Strong final note.

tmdb_overview: Jeff accepts an invitation to be the editor of the school paper as he and his friends fend off an interloper who wants to join their study group.
insight: Solid character comedy carries a mid-tier episode through 70 jokes in 23 minutes.
